title: Not in our power, yet we can hinder it: Alvarez's man commanded to fly
source_text: L. Porro Doctores illi agnoscunt istam Dei motionem ad omne bonum opus praeviam & necessariam in potestate hominis non esse; quia datur & negatur ex divino beneplacito. Sed nihilominus affirmant in facultate nostrae voluntatis esse seipsam impedire ne habeat motionem illam. Unde colligunt quod, si non operetur actum, qui est in praecepto, imputabitur illi ad culpam, eo quod sua culpa se impedivit, ne daretur illi auxilium efficax, quod necessarium erat, ut actualiter operaretur actum virtutis, qui est in praecepto: sicut si Deus imponeret homini praeceptum volandi, & quantum est ex parte sua, offerret illi alas, & adjutorium necessarium ut volaret; ipse autem sua libertate responderet; Domine nec volo alas accipere nec volare; merito reputaretur reus, & transgressor praecepti, etiamsi non posset absque alis volare, quia sua culpa se impedivit, ne illi donarentur a Deo. Quae sunt verba ejusdem Alvarez libri jamjam citati disputatione decima octava num. 20. Ubi suam doctrinam confirmat Augustini dicto, Ut homines non adjuventur gratia Dei, in ipsis causa est, non in Deo.
pass_a_gloss: L. Further those Doctors acknowledge that that motion of God prior and necessary for every good work is not in the power of man; because it is given and denied from the divine good pleasure. But nevertheless they affirm that it is in the faculty of our will to hinder itself so that it not have that motion. Whence they gather that, if he does not work the act, which is in the precept, it will be imputed to him for fault, because by his fault he hindered himself, so that the efficacious help was not given him, which was necessary, that he might actually work the act of virtue, which is in the precept: as if God imposed on a man the precept of flying, and as much as is on his part, offered him wings, and the help necessary that he might fly; but he by his liberty should answer; Lord I neither will to receive wings nor to fly; deservedly he would be reputed guilty, and a transgressor of the precept, even if he could not fly without wings, because by his fault he hindered himself, so that they were not given him by God. Which are the words of the same Alvarez in the book just now cited disputation eighteenth num. 20. Where he confirms his doctrine by the saying of Augustine, That men are not helped by the grace of God, the cause is in themselves, not in God.
pass_b_english: Thesis L. These doctors also acknowledge that this motion of God, prior to and necessary for every good work, is not in a person's power, since it is given and withheld at God's good pleasure. Yet they maintain that our will has the capacity to prevent itself from receiving that motion.

From this they infer: 'If a person does not perform the act that is commanded, it will be counted against him as a fault, because by his own fault he prevented the efficacious aid from being given him, which he needed in order actually to perform the act of virtue that is commanded. It is as if God laid on someone a command to fly and, as far as lay with God, offered him wings and the help he needed to fly, and the man answered in his freedom, "Lord, I do not want to take wings or to fly": he would rightly be held guilty and a breaker of the command, even though he could not fly without wings, because by his own fault he prevented their being given him by God.'

These are the words of the same Alvarez in the book just cited, disputation 18, section 20, where he supports his teaching with Augustine's saying: 'That people are not helped by God's grace, the cause lies in themselves, not in God.'
